podcast.title: New Wave Powerpop
podcast.body: The Records are listed among the artists who contributed to the new wave take on Powerpop. They exemplify the integration of catchy melodies and sharp guitar work with the energy and attitude influenced by punk, marking Powerpop's entry into the alternative rock sphere. "We had the cars, the shoes, the records, the buzz cocks, Elvis Costello and Joe Jackson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Artistic Control in Modern Recordings
xref.body: Having learned from past experiences where they questioned management and production decisions, The Headstones now exert full control over their recording process. This autonomy is seen as crucial, with the band believing their newer records, made under their complete direction, are superior and more authentically represent their sound. "That's why now when we make the records, we control everything. And these records to me are the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Hardcore Vinyl Fan
xref.body: Eddie Vedder, frontman for Pearl Jam, is noted as a "hardcore vinyl fan." This detail was highlighted when his band's song "Let The Records Play" was featured after a discussion about the invention and significant impact of vinyl records on the music industry. "Hardcore, vinyl fan, Eddie Vetter, with Pearl Jam and Let The Records Play from the Lightning Bold album from 2013."

xref.title: Influence on "Twice Removed"
xref.body: Fleetwood Mac was among the artists Sloan members were listening to while creating "Twice Removed," contributing to the album's shift towards a quieter, more poppy sound. "I think some of the records that we're listening to more were like Fleetwood Mac or the third Velvet Underground album, which is sort of quieter records, you know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influenced by The Stooges
xref.body: Sonic Youth cited The Stooges as one of the records that shaped their sound in the 1980s. "If you traveled back to the 80s and ask Sonic Youth about the records that shaped their sound, they would probably say the stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Multi-Instrumentalist Producer
xref.body: Chris Berkett became a multi-instrumentalist (piano, bass, drums, guitar) to effectively communicate with musicians in the studio, often by demonstrating desired grooves or parts directly on the instrument rather than solely relying on written scores or verbal explanations. "I had to learn piano, bass, drums, and play, and then to play everything so that I could communicate with the musicians that are making the records in the right way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New Wave Powerpop
xref.body: The Cars are identified as one of the new wave bands that embraced Powerpop, integrating its spiky, angular, fun, and sing-along song structures into their sound. They are grouped with other artists who blended punk influences into the Powerpop formula, contributing to its integration into alternative rock. "We had the cars, the shoes, the records, the buzz cocks, Elvis Costello and Joe Jackson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New Wave Powerpop
xref.body: The Shoes are mentioned as one of the bands that defined the new wave brand of Powerpop. Their sound reflects the post-punk era, taking the energetic, melodic, and hook-driven characteristics of Powerpop and blending them with new wave sensibilities, showcasing punk's influence. "We had the cars, the shoes, the records, the buzz cocks, Elvis Costello and Joe Jackson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New Wave Powerpop with Punk Influence
xref.body: The Buzzcocks are cited as a band that incorporated elements of punk into the new wave brand of Powerpop. Their sound, along with contemporaries like Elvis Costello and Joe Jackson, helped define the integration of Powerpop into the alternative rock world. "We had the cars, the shoes, the records, the buzz cocks, Elvis Costello and Joe Jackson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Touring Before Stardom
xref.body: Alexis on Fire toured with Avenged Sevenfold right before Avenged Sevenfold signed their major label deals and released the records that would launch them into superstardom. This tour offered a glimpse into the major label courting process and the impending surge in popularity for aggressive music. "I remember we did a, we did a long American tour with, it was us, Mike him and Evan Sevenfold, both right before both those, like both of them have just signed their major label deals and both had made the records that would then propel them into super stardom, but it was the tour right before that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

xref.title: Unauthorized "New York Vocal Mix"
xref.body: DJ Francois Cervorcian's "New York vocal mix" of "This Charming Man" was initially created without proper permission from The Smiths, leading to the records being withdrawn. This unauthorized 12-inch version became highly sought after in the 1980s, described as "like gold," before an agreement was reached for its official release in 1992. "Unfortunately, he never got the proper permission from the Smiths and the records were withdrawn."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
